chunks: "The values come from the E-series, which are preferred numbers spaced logarithmically in each decade.
E12 has 12 values per decade, 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82, and those pair with 10 percent parts.
E24 has 24 values, with things like 11, 13, 16, 20, 24, 30, and goes with 5 percent. E96 has 96 values per decade, like 100, 102, 105, 107, and goes with 1 percent parts.
The spacing is chosen so neighbors overlap within tolerance, which means any value you want is within the tolerance of a standard one.
The values I reach for most are 10 ohms, 100, 1k, 4. 7k, 10k, 100k, and 1 meg, plus 0 ohm jumpers, 22 and 33 ohms for series termination, 220 to 470 for LEDs, 2. 2k and 4.
7k for I2C, and 49. 9 ohm for 50-ohm terminations, which is an E96 value. In practice I'd choose the series by how accurate the ratio or value needs to be.
For a feedback divider I'd use 1 percent E96 or 0. 1 percent so I can hit the target, and then compute the actual output with the real values instead of the ideal ones."
